Discussion

Recurrent intestinal inflammation has detrimental effects on the physical and mental health of patients with UC. UC may not cause irreversible damage, such as Crohn disease (CD), although it is still a serious disease. Although current clinical treatments have led to cases of remission, biologics are expensive, and treatment is often ineffective or leads to serious side effects. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify medications with fewer side effects, better quality, and lower costs. In recent years, researchers have begun to study how different traditional Chinese medicine compounds alleviate UC. Their aim was to identify alternative treatments that are affordable and have fewer adverse effects. Research revealed that a compound derived from Chinese yam significantly reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines associated with UC, suppresses the activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, and promotes the restoration of tight junction protein expression in the intestinal lining. Berberine can inhibit the excessive activation of macrophages to modulate immune responses, and it regulates the composition and function of the intestinal microbiota and enhances the functionality of the intestinal barrier. These multiple mechanisms indicate that berberine may represent a viable and promising option for the treatment of UC. Rhein helps alleviate intestinal inflammation in UC by acting on the gut microbiota and lowering uric acid levels. Although the aforementioned traditional Chinese medicine monomers may have the potential to alleviate UC, the mechanisms of many other components remain inadequately understood. These unexplored components may act through various pathways, including inhibition of inflammation, regulation of immune function, and protection of the intestinal barrier. Therefore, additional studies are required to thoroughly investigate the mechanisms underlying the effects of these traditional Chinese medicine constituents, determine their specific roles in the treatment of UC, and identify the optimal methods for their use.

GLA was first isolated in 1981. Since then, it has been found to exhibit inflammation-modulating, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-neutralizing, antitumor and immunoregulatory effects. GLA inhibits the advancement of osteoarthritis (OA) in both in vivo and in vitro models by blocking the activation of the NF-kappaB and MAPK pathways and significantly downregulating the expression of IL-1beta and PGE231. GLA reduces the concentration of inflammatory mediators in CCl4-induced liver fibrosis and helps restore the balance of the gut microbiota. GLA also limits multiple myeloma cell proliferation by targeting and repressing STAT3 expression, which helps slow the progression of multiple myeloma. GLA is a broadly applicable natural active formula with great potential for applications in anti-inflammatory, antitumor, and immunoregulatory therapies. Because of its broad functionality, this compound is a promising candidate for application in various fields. However, the potential benefits and underlying mechanisms of GLA in the treatment of IBD have not yet been investigated. Thus, further research is required to thoroughly explore its roles in treating IBD. This is the first study to explore the ability of GLA to alleviate colonic inflammation. Acute UC was induced in mice using 3% DSS, and intraperitoneal injections of GLA at 20 and 40 mg/kg were administered to the treatment groups daily. The results revealed that GLA alleviated symptoms such as shortened colon length, loose stools, and weight loss in mice. Histopathological analysis showed that GLA suppressed colonic and glandular structure damage, crypt loss, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Thus, our findings revealed that GLA effectively alleviated acute UC in mice. Furthermore, our results indicate that the histological scores in the GLA 40 mg/kg group were improved compared to those in the 20 mg/kg group; however, the clinical DAI scores on days 6-7 showed the opposite trend, possibly due to the optimal therapeutic concentration of GLA. Next, we will further investigate the maximum safe dose of GLA for treating UC.

To further investigate the mechanism by which GLA alleviates colonic inflammation, we performed immunohistochemical staining, which revealed that GLA treatment diminished the expression of MPO and F4/80 in mouse colonic tissues. F4/80 is a specific glycoprotein marker that is widely present in tissue-resident macrophages in mice, and it is commonly used to study the distribution and function of macrophages. The higher its positive expression, the more severe the intestinal inflammation. Excessive macrophage activation is a key feature of IBD. Macrophages in the intestine are highly adaptable and can differentiate into two polarized states depending on environmental changes. When intestinal inflammation occurs, macrophages tend to secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1beta, and TNF-alpha, thereby exacerbating the inflammation. Simultaneously, some macrophages release inhibitory cytokines such as IL-10 to help alleviate inflammation. The GLA-induced alleviation of UC may be related to the modulation of macrophage function by GLA, as evidenced by the expression levels of inflammatory cytokines in the colonic tissues of the mice. To further explore the mechanism underlying the anti-colitis effects of GLA, we conducted a network pharmacology analysis. The key shared target between GLA and inflammatory bowel disease is AKT. mTOR is an important downstream protein of the PI3K/AKT pathway closely related to an overreaction of immune cells in many autoimmune diseases. Our experimental findings suggest GLA's anti-inflammatory activity may involve modulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. Previous studies have shown that GLA can alleviate RANKL-induced inflammation in RAW264.7 cells by inhibiting the activation of AKT. This suggests the potential mechanism underlying its anti-inflammatory effects. AKT acts as a primary effector of PI3K and is a vital component of the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade, which is crucial for regulating cellular growth, proliferation, and metabolism. In acute UC in mice, the AKT signaling pathway can activate macrophages, thereby influencing both the intensity and duration of the inflammatory response. The abnormal activation of the AKT/PI3K pathway in macrophages results in excessive intestinal inflammation and tissue damage. Therefore, we established an LPS-induced inflammation model using macrophages. LPS induces the expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6 by activating downstream signaling pathways by binding to TLR4 on the surface of macrophages. In this study, PCR was used to assess the mRNA expression of various inflammatory factors in the cellular models. The results demonstrated that the expression of these inflammatory factors significantly decreased in the groups treated with different concentrations of GLA, which was attributed to the regulation of the AKT pathway. This decrease may be attributed to the GLA-mediated inhibition of AKT signaling, which weakened the transmission of inflammatory signals. Inhibition of AKT signaling may further suppress the activation of downstream transcription factors such as NF-kappaB, thereby leading to a decrease in the transcription levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes. Western blot analysis revealed that the proteins associated with the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway were upregulated in LPS-treated RAW264.7 cells, which was significantly reversed upon GLA treatment. Our findings suggest that GLA may regulate macrophage function by inhibiting PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, thereby reducing the mRNA expression of the inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1beta, and TNF-alpha.

Studies have shown that macrophages derived from monocyte differentiation are more abundant in the intestine. Therefore, we selected peripheral blood samples from patients with active UC to extract high-purity monocytes (> 95% purity). In this study, treatment with GLA (10 microM) significantly reduced the IL-6 and IL-1beta levels in monocytes from UC patients but notably increased the IL-10 levels. Through animal experiments, cell studies, network pharmacology, and human peripheral blood analysis, we collectively confirmed that GLA can alleviate IBD symptoms by inhibiting macrophage activation via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. In addition, GLA is inexpensive and readily available, thus offering a new approach to the clinical treatment of patients with IBD.

However, to date, no studies have directly compared GLA with the current commonly used UC therapeutics in clinical practice. To better assess the relative efficacy of GLA, future studies will need to systematically compare it with these standard treatment regimens. Owing to GLA's low polarity, poor water solubility, rapid elimination from the body, short half-life, and low bioavailability, it cannot be directly used as a drug in clinical settings. Currently, numerous studies have adopted nanocarriers to encapsulate traditional Chinese medicine monomers as a solution to such issues. Genistein (GEN) has shown potential in preventing and alleviating colitis,however, its clinical application is significantly limited by its low water solubility and bioavailability. Previous studies have demonstrated that the use of nanocarriers (GEN-NP2) can enhance its bioavailability while maintaining its chemical stability and enabling controlled release at the site of pathology. Berberine (BBR) also exhibits protective and alleviative effects against colonic inflammation. Due to its low bioavailability in vivo, researchers have synthesized BBR-loaded carboxymethyl chitosan nanoparticles, which have demonstrated targeted therapeutic efficacy in ameliorating murine colitis. These nano-drug delivery systems have significantly enhanced bioavailability. Previous studies have demonstrated that GLA-loaded nanoparticles exhibit superior anti-tumor activity both in vitro and in vivo. Building on these evidences, we are actively developing advanced delivery strategies, including nanoparticle encapsulation or prodrug modification, to optimize GLA's pharmacokinetic profile for IBD treatment. More suitable delivery methods need to be explored, and considerable work must be performed before this therapeutic strategy can be applied in clinical practice.
Conclusion

Our previous research revealed that GLA can alleviate UC by reducing the levels of inflammatory cytokines. Thus, in the present study, we investigated a mouse inflammation model, RAW264.7 cell model, and human peripheral blood samples and found that GLA reduced the mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines while increasing the mRNA expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines. GLA also reduced the expression of MPO and F4/80 in colon tissues and inhibited LPS-induced phosphorylation and activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways. Therefore, GLA has significant potential as a therapeutic agent for treating IBD and may offer new treatment options for autoimmune diseases.

passages.text: A sustainable approach in pumpkin seed oil processing line: Recent advances in pumpkin seed oil and oil processing by-products

Pumpkin seed oil (PSO) has gained popularity worldwide for its nutritional profile and biological effects, significantly increasing its market demand and consumption. However, pumpkin seed oil cake (PSOC), as the secondary by-product from oil processing, contains high potential value and is scarcely utilised. With the PSO increase in production, a large amount of PSOC will be generated. The key to achieving a sustainable food system is maximising value from the food supply chain. This review aims to summarise the nutritional profile of PSO and PSOC and highlight the current advance in the biological activity of PSO and the valorisation strategies of PSOC. This review also concludes the current advance in food applications of PSO and PSOC in meat and bakery products, respectively. A better understanding of their value and current advances can help to achieve the maximisimg value from PSO processing line in an effective and sustainable approach.
Highlights
Nutritional profile and biological effects of pumpkin seed oil.
Nutritional value and utilisation strategies of pumpkin seed oil cake.
Applications of pumpkin seed oil and its oil cake in food.
Maximising value from pumpkin seed oil processing line for sustainability.
Introduction

Pumpkin, belonging to the Cucurbitaceae family, is an important vegetable widely cultivated in the world. The most commercially cultivated pumpkin species are Cucurbita pepo, Cucurbita maxima, and Cucurbita moschata. According to the data from FAOSTAT (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Statistical Analysis) in 2022, the annual pumpkin worldwide production is around 23 million tons, whereas the largest production region in Asia (50.5 %), followed by Europe (21.2 %), Americas (15.4 %), Africa (11.9 %), and Oceania (1.0 %). The global production of pumpkin seed, which accounts for 4 % to 6 % of total weight of the pumpkin, is estimated to be around 0.92-1.38 million tons. Pumpkin seed is commonly used as food ingredient and for oil production, of this, approximately 4.9 % is used for the production of pumpkin seed oil.
The Wasted Food Scale from United States Environmental Protection Agency.
Fig. 1

Pumpkin seed oil (PSO) has received much attention due to its nutritional value and biological effects. PSO contains high level of unsaturated fatty acid and other biological compounds, such as phytosterols, squalene, tocopherols, and carotenoids; in addition, many studies have shown that the potential of PSO in intestinal parasites, prostate, and hair loss treatment. The market demand and consumption of PSO are increasing, and the PSO market is expected to reach USD 2.07 billion by 2030, with a GAGR of 10.4 % during period 2024 to 2030. PSO in the market is usually obtained through traditionally pressed method (e.g. cold and hot pressed) and solvent extraction method. Besides, other novel extraction methods, including supercritical fluid extraction, aqueous enzymatic extraction, and ultrasonic assisted extraction have been employed in PSO extraction. Notably, during oil processing, pumpkin seed oil cake (PSOC), the secondary by-product of pumpkin seed oil, is generally discarded or converted into animal feed. However, this utilisation strategy is not the most effective approach, since oil cake contains high potential value, such as protein, fibre, phenolics, and minerals, which can be re-utilised. According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) developed the Wasted Food Scale (Fig. 1), if the food by-products cannot be avoided, the most effective approach is to recover and re-utilise them as food ingredients to feed people (the second tier in Fig. 1). Additionally, many studies have reported that oil cake has great for re-introducing into food chain as a promising ingredient to fortify the nutritional profile of food products. On the other hand, the above utilisation approach also can reduce food waste and enhance food system resilience, which is in line with sustainable development goals (SDG), such as SDG 2 (zero hunger) and SDG 12 (ensure sustainable production and consumption). Therefore, to better help to maximise the value of pumpkin seed in the oil production line, it is important to understand the value of PSO and PSOC and their current advances.

In this context, this review aims to summarise and highlight the nutritional profile of PSO and PSOC, the biological effects of PSO, and the current popular valorisation strategy of PSOC. Besides, this review also concludes the current advances in food applications of both. Overall, this review could provide useful information to promote a complete valorisation of pumpkin seed oil processing lines and build a more sustainable and resource-efficient food system.

PSO contains numerous nutritional compounds, which associates with its biological activities. This section presents the nutritional profile of PSO.

Table 1 presents the fatty acid profile of PSO. PSO is rich in unsaturated fatty acid (UFA), where oleic acid (C18:1; 21.0 % - 46.75 %) and linoleic acid (C18:2; 32.57 % - 60.6 %) are major fatty acids. In terms of saturated fatty acid (SFA) in PSO, palmitic acid (C16:0; 10.0 % - 19.08 %) and stearic acid (C18:0; 5.16 % - 10.98 %) are major fatty acids. Besides, PSO is detected to contain low levels of ALA (alpha-linolenic acid; C18:3 n-3; 0.03 % - 0.7 %) and GLA (gamma-linolenic acid; C18:3 n-6; 0.33 % - 0.4 %), indicating that its potential nutritional value. Studies have been indicated that ALA and GLA are bioactive components, which have potential biological benefits for human health, such as cardioprotective and colorectal cancer prevention. On the other hand, the fatty acid of PSO could be influenced by environmental factors (e.g. climate, soil, and cultivation area), genotype (e.g. pumpkin variety), and extraction methods, especially in the content of oleic acid (C18:1) and linoleic acid (C18:2). investigated the effect of extraction methods on fatty acid profile of PSOC, three extraction methods, including cold-pressed, microwave pretreatment, and supercritical fluid) were employed. They found that the PSO obtained from cold-pressed had highest SFA content (27.31 %) and lowest UFA content (72.69 %), while PSO obtained from supercritical fluid extraction had highest UFA content (75.86 %) and lowest SFA content (24.14 %). Similarly, extracted PSO using three extraction methods (solvent extraction, cold-pressed extraction, and aqueous enzymatic extraction) and found that extraction method affected fatty acid profile of PSOC: solvent extraction (oleic acid 21 %, linoleic acid 61.9 %) and cold-pressed extraction (oleic acid 34.1 %, linoleic acid 47.9 %) showed the highest linoleic and oleic acids, respectively. According to and, the properties or structures of fatty acids have different responses to different extraction conditions (e.g. solvent type and temperature). Besides, analysed 928 samples of PSO (Cucurbita pepo L.) from Croatia, Slovenia, Austria, and Hungary, and found that geographical location had a significant effect on the ratio of oleic acid (C18:1) to linoleic acid (C18:2), with the PSO obtained from Austria had a lower ratio than PSO obtained from Croatia and Slovenia. This variation could be attributed to climate conditions. Climate conditions (e.g. temperature) determine fatty acid accumulation during plant growth, the change in climate conditions cause adaptive responses, thereby affecting the fatty acid accumulation Notably, the genotype is also an important factor influencing fatty acid accumulation in plants, since different varieties could respond differently to the same climate conditions.

PSO also contains various bioactive compounds, mainly including phytosterols, tocopherols, squalene, and carotenoids, which have various health benefits and contribute to their biological activities. The bioactive compounds of PSO are listed in Table 2.
Phytosterols

Phytosterols are natural bioactive compounds widely found in plants, which have a variety of health benefits (e.g. cholesterol-lowering, preventing cardiovascular diseases, and anti-inflammatory), and their structural similarity to cholesterol. detected 14 phytosterols in PSO (Cucurbita maxima, obtained from Tunisia), namely campesterol, campestanol, cholesterol, clerosterol, stigmasterol, sitosterol, sitostanol, Delta5-avenasterol, 24-methylenecholesterol, Delta5,23-stigmastadienol, Delta5,24-stigmastadienol, Delta7-campesterol, Delta7-stigmastenol, and Delta7-avenasterol. As shown in Table 2, among the reported phytosterols in PSO, beta-sitosterol (49.25-208.2 mg/100 g oil) was the major phytosterol. Notably, according to, Delta7-sterols were specific phytosterols in PSO and could be as identification markers to detect PSO authenticity. Besides, as shown in Table 2, the content and components of phytosterols in PSO can be affected by genotype and environmental factors. Except the above factors, the process of PSO extraction can also influence the phytosterols content. Furthermore, investigated the effect of pretreatment methods (microwave and roasting) on the phytosterols content of cold-pressed PSO, the results showed that the PSO obtained from cold-pressed with pretreatments (microwave for 598.9 mg/100 g oil and roasting for 715.6 mg/100 g oil) had higher phytosterol content than control (473.5 mg/100 g oil; cold-pressed without pretreatment).
Tocopherols

Tocopherols are important lipophilic antioxidants in widely plant oils, which are classified into four types, i.e., alpha-tocopherol, beta-tocopherol, gamma-tocopherol, and delta-tocopherol. As can be seen from Table 2, alpha, gamma, and delta are the most common types of tocopherols in PSO. Additionally, Singh & Kumar and detected the presence of beta-tocopherol isomer in PSO, ranged from 0.61 to 7.10 (mg/100 g oil). Notably, the content of tocopherols and the ratio of isomers in PSO can be affected by multiple factors, such as pumpkin genotype and environmental conditions (e.g. soil, climate, and location), as shown in Table 2. For example, analysed the tocopherol content in two varieties of PSO (Cucurbita moschata Duchesne and Cucurbita argyrosperma Huber) obtained from Yucatan, Mexico. They reported that delta-tocopherol (32.87-41.78 mg/100 g oil) was most predominant tocopherol in PSO, followed by alpha-tocopherol (1.29-3.75 mg/100 g oil) and gamma-tocopherol (0.54-1.52 mg/100 g oil). In contrast, in study, who detected PSO (Cucurbita pepo L. subsp. pepo var. styriaca Greb.) obtained from Poland and the content of gamma-tocopherol (37.74 mg/100 g oil) was found to be the highest among three types of tocopherols identified (alpha-tocopherol and delta-tocopherol were 0.43 mg/100 g oil and 0.12 mg/100 g oil, respectively).
Squalene

Squalene, a nature polyunsaturated triterpenoid compound widely presents in various oils, has many biological activities, such as anti-aging in skin, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and cholesterol-lowering). The content of squalene in PSO ranges from 116.0 to 283.58 (mg/100 g oil), depending on pumpkin variety and growing location (Table 2). Compared with other conventional diet oils, PSO is similar to olive oil (234.75-393.2 mg/100 g oil), but higher than sunflower oil (12.56-18.68 mg/100 g oil), rapeseed oil (3.42-5.70 mg/100 g oil), soybean oil (5.84-13.74 mg/100 g oil), and sesame oil (0.99.- 8.76 mg/100 g oil). The above suggests that PSO is a potential good source of squalene.
Carotenoids

Carotenoids are natural lipophilic antioxidants and bioactivity compounds, which are important to human nutrition and health (e.g. preventing neurodegenerative diseases and health of the eyes). and reported that PSO contained beta-carotene (0.04-0.38 mg/100 g oil) and lutein (0.04-0.21 mg/100 g oil). Besides, identified 5 carotenoids in PSO, including beta-carotene (0.69 mg/100 g oil); alpha-carotene (0.24 mg/100 g oil); zeaxanthin (0.25 mg/100 g oil); violaxanthin (0.47 mg/100 g oil), and lutein epoxide (1.85 mg/100 g oil), whereas beta-carotene content was higher than and studies. This difference could be attributed to the pumpkin variety, growing factors, and extraction methods.

PSO has various health benefits, such as antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory, anthelmintic effect, anti-hyperplastic effect, neuroprotective effect, and against alopecia. These biological activities could be attributed to the bioactive compounds in PSO, as mentioned above. Table 3 concludes the current advances in biological activity of PSO. Many studies have demonstrated the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of PSO, which can be attributed to its bioactivity compounds, such as squalene, tocopherols, phytosterols, and among others. evaluated the antioxidant capacity of PSO extracts through in vitro chemical assay (DPPH and ABTS), and shown that PSO extracts had good antioxidant capacity (DPPH assay as 15.25 mg Trolox equivalent/100 mL sample and ABTS as 22.90 mg Trolox equivalent/100 mL sample). There is also evidence to indicate antioxidant capacity of PSO in animal model. reported that PSO can contributed to reduction of alleviate heat stress-induced oxidative damage in rabbit model, in which male rabbits were supplied PSO in their daily diet at 2.0 mL/kg diet for 8 weeks. In terms of anti-inflammatory, indicated the anti-inflammatory activity of PSO (IC50 = 6.25 mug/mL) through in vitro chemical method (by determining the inhibition of serum bovine albumin denaturation), which was higher than control (diclofenac sodium, IC50 = 5.47 mug/mL).

Trichinellosis, also referred to as trichinosis, is a parasitic infection caused by Trichinella spiralis; most of human infections are caused by consuming uncooked meat (common in pork) that carries encysted Trichinella spiralis larvae. The conventional treatment drugs are albendazole and mebendazole, however, these drugs could cause many side effects, such as headaches, fever, anemia, and pancytopenia. Therefore, finding safe and natural alternative drugs are necessary. In a study by, treatment with PSO showed a significant effect on the reduction of parasite in terms of the number of adults and encysted larvae in the infected mice model; in addition, PSO exhibited the potential anti-inflammatory through reducing MMP-9 (matrix metalloproteinase-9) levels in intestinal and muscular tissues from infected mice.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a common chronic disease in the aging men population (beginning around 50 years old), results in begin enlargement of prostate gland followed by bladder outlet obstruction; presenting as lower urinary tract symptoms (e.g. weakness of urinary stream and hesitancy initiating flow). In study, who used phytosterol extracts from PSO as treatment to evaluate its effect on inhibition of BPH in the animal model (rats), they found that the PSO phytosterol extracts treatment (1 mL per day per rat) for 4 weeks can ameliorated the pathological prostate enlargement in BPH induced rats, with the prostate weight of the former (treated group using PSO extracts, 875.1 mg) was lower than the latter (BPH induced group, 1072.9 mg). In another single-blind randomised clinical study, treated BPH patients using tamsulosin and PSO. The results showed that PSO treatment (360 mg, twice per day) for 3 months can relieved BPH symptoms assessed by IPSS (international prostate symptom score). Although PSO treatment was not as effective as tamsulosin (alpha blockers), the former treatment did not cause any sides effect.
Besides that, PSO exhibits the effects on neuroprotective effects and against alopecia.

In terms of neuroprotective effect, the animal study shown that PSO exhibited prophylactic effect on neuro-inflammatory interactions in the ovariectomised rat model. In terms of against alopecia, PSO showed promising potential in male mice model and results showed that the PSO orally (1 mL/kg) for 14 days or topically (10 muL) for 7 days can acted in the proliferation of the hair follicles and without toxicity in the liver.

passages.text: Pumpkin seed oil cake from oil processing

Considering the above context, pumpkin seed is largely used to obtain pumpkin seed oil; during the pumpkin seed oil processing, pumpkin oil processing by-product, known as press cake (i.e. pumpkin seed oil cake; PSOC) is generated after oil extraction, and which also contains potential nutritional value (e.g. protein, fibre, minerals, and phenolics). Valorisation of PSOC into high value-added products, which in line with sustainable food development and circular economy strategies, thus, developing comprehensive utilisation of PSOC has received much attention, such as re-introducing in food supply chain as food ingredient and the extraction of high value-added compounds. In this section, the compositions of PSOC and its current advance in high value-added compounds extraction are concluded.

Phenolic compounds, the secondary metabolites produced in widely plants, are important functional bioactive substances in human life.. These compounds have been exhibited several potentially biological properties, such as antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial. PSOC also is potential good source of phenolic compounds. The total phenolic content (TPC) of PSOC ranges from 230 to 4089 (mg gallic acid equivalent/100 g), depending on extraction methods and conditions, and pumpkin variety. studied the subcritical water extraction method with different solvents on the extraction of phenolic compounds from PSOC, three different solvents (N2, N2 with 0.05 mol/L of HCl, and CO2) were employed under the constant other conditions (the solid to solvent ratio of 1:30 (w/v) at 160  C and 20 bar for 30 min). The global plant-based food market is growing at CAGR of 12.4 % from 2022 to 2929 and is expected to reach USD 99.52 billion by 2029. The requirement and consumption of plant-based protein is increasing, PSOC has been carried out on the protein extraction as an alternative source of plant-based protein. Table 6 concludes the current advance on protein extraction from PSOC. From a nutritional point of view, PS protein contains 9 essential amino acids, which leucine (6.44 % - 7.82 %, w/w of protein), valine (4.10 % - 5.60 %, w/w of protein), phenylalanine (4.51 % - 5.32 %, w/w of protein), and Isoleucine (4.14 % - 4.28 %, w/w of protein) are abundant. In addition, glutamic acid (20.70 % - 21.03 %, w/w of protein), arginine (16.04 % - 18.58 %, w/w of protein), and aspartic acid (7.04 % - 8.83 %, w/w of protein) are major non-essential amino acids. Besides, PS protein has also known desirable functional properties, including water holding, foaming, emulsifying, and gelling capacity, which can be considered as functional ingredient in food development.

Based on this context, PSO and its oil processing by-products (pumpkin seed oil cake; PSOC) have been introduced into food supply chain and utilised as potentially nutritional ingredient for development of novel sustainable food products. Table 7 summarises the current advance in the utilisation and application of PSO and pumpkin seed oil cake (PSOC) in food product development.
Application of PSO in food
The recent exploration of PSO-added food prototypes including burger, sausage, and meatball, whereas PSO is mainly as animal fat replacer and antioxidant for above products (Table 7).

The fatty acid composition and bioactivity compounds of PSO make it efficient functional ingredient to improve the fatty composition of meat products and provide potential health effects. developed a novel dried-fermented sausage ('fuet') using PSO emulsion as pork fat replacer at 50 %, 75 %, and 100 % replacing level. The sausage made with 75 % of PSO or above can decreased SFA content and increased PUFA (mainly in linoleic acid content) compared to control (100 % pork fat sausage). In terms of colour and texture, PSO addition increased redness (a*), yellowness (b*), and springiness value, but decreased the hardness of the sausage. Finally, the reformulated sausage product had a lower sensory score than control in terms of appearance, taste, odour, and texture. Similarly, in another study that has used PSO emulsion as animal fat replacer in burger, the results shown that an increase in redness (a*) and yellowness (b*), while texture properties (hardness, elasticity, cohesiveness, and chewiness) decreased. In terms of nutritional profile, the protein and vitamin E content of reformulated burger increased, and fat content decreased. Regarding with the fatty acid profile, the content of SFA and MUFA (mainly in oleic acid) decreased, while the PUFA (mainly in linoleic acid) content increased. Besides, in sensory evaluation, although all reformulated burgers decreased the texture and taste scores, the external aspect score increased.

In addition to the above, PSO has also been studied as an antioxidant ingredient to inhibit the formation of heterocyclic aromatic amines (HAAs) in cooked meat products. HAAs are Maillard reaction derivatives and classified as carcinogens, which are produced during thermal processing of high protein products, including baking, roasting, smoking, and frying. One study from, who added PSO in meatballs at 1 % and 2 % of total meatball weight and investigated its inhibitory effects on HAAs formation. The results showed that PSO addition can reduced the HAAs formation in pan-fried (10 min) and roasted meatballs (7 min) at cooking temperature between 150  C to 250  C, with the reduction rate reaching 76.25 % in pan-fried meatballs and 19.95 % in roasted meatballs at the highest temperature.
Application of PSOC in food
As mentioned earlier, PSOC, as a valuable ingredient, is a good source of protein, fibre, minerals, and phenolic compounds, offering the opportunity to enrich the nutritional value of these products.

reported that the addition of PSOC improved the pasta nutritional profile in terms of protein content, ash, oil, total phenolic content, and antioxidant capacity. Regarding with physical parameters of pasta, PSOC addition increased hardness and greenness and decreased lightness. Considering all the parameters of pasta, reformulated paste with 9 % PSOC had the overall good sensory scores. Similarly, PSOC was used to fortified bread nutritional value by. They found that PSOC addition increased protein, ash, and fibre content in bread, and 10 % PSOC addition had the highest sensory score among all bread products.

The PSOC was used in gluten-free crackers formulation. used two types of PSOC (cold-pressed and thermal pre-treatment before pressed) replaced chickpea flour at 20 % (w/w) and 35 % (w/w) replacing level and 100 % chickpea cracker as control. The results shown that PSOC addition increased protein and minerals (e.g. magnesium, iron, and zinc) content in crackers. After in vitro digestion, except for cracker made with 35 % cold-pressed PSOC, the protein digestibility of reformulated crackers (59.56 % - 74.86 %) were lower than control (76.97 %). This could be attributed to the phenolics in PSOC, which bind to proteins inhibit access to digestive enzymes.

used PSOC as bioactive ingredient to enrich the nutritional value of wafers. They reported that PSOC addition changed the functional properties of wafers in terms of water holding capacity (WHC) and oil holding capacity (OHC), whereas WHC decreased and OHC increased with increasing PSOC addition. PSOC addition did not significantly changed (p > 0.05) the hardness, but caused wafer colour to darker. Regarding with nutritional changed, the total phenolic content and antioxidant capacity were increased.

Apart from the above, PS protein extracted from PSOC has been used in several food applications. For example, added PS protein (5 %, 10 %, and 20 % of total wheat flour weight) in bread production, the results showed that PS addition did not affect (p > 0.05) the gas holding and shape hold capacity of the dough and increased the protein content of bread; in addition, bread contained up to 10 % PS protein had similar scores compared to control bread (without PS protein addition) in terms of bread quality evaluation (e.g. colour, aroma, taste, chewability of crumb, and appearance). Additionally, developed the low-fat cheddar cheese using PS protein-based double emulsions (25 % wt. protein concentration, water-in-oil-in-water). They found that cheese made with PS protein-based double emulsion had significantly lower (p < 0.05) hardness and oil loss than control (low-fat cheddar cheese) after 14 days of maturation.
The potential application of PSO in cosmetics

Considering the nutritional profile and biological activities of PSO, it also has been used as a promising ingredient for development of novel cosmetics. Investigated the potential of PSO in photoprotection cosmetic application and found that incorporation of PSO in formulation increased the photoprotective properties. developed PSO-based vitamin E cream formulation for topical application to nourish the skin and the results showed that PSO addition improved the antioxidant activity of the formulation, with the formulation containing 20 % PSO had highest antioxidant activity. formulated makeup remover using PSO and results showed that the remover containing PSO did not cause skin irritation and performed better than the comparator in terms of makeup removal ability.
Conclusions and future perspectives

PSO contains high level of UFA (mainly in oleic acid and linoleic acid) and is also rich in other biological compounds such as squalene, phytosterols, tocopherols, and carotenoids, which have been reported to exhibit excellent biological activities (e.g. antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and Inhibition of benign prostatic hyperplasia) in in vitro and in vivo studies. However, it is unclear the mechanism of its various biological activities and the corresponding compounds, the potential concentration limits of its use, and the question of safety. Therefore, more studies are needed to discover this field. Additionally, regarding with PSO in food application, PSO exhibits its potential as an animal fat replacer in the development of healthy meat products. However, it should be emphasized that the use of fat replacer can significantly changes the physical properties of meat products, including texture, colour, and appearance, which could affect sensory properties and consumer acceptance. Therefore, optimising the incorporation level of PSO or combination of PSO with other ingredients to produce meat products with desirable quality is important in further studies.

Besides, PSOC, as a major by-product of PSO processing, contains high potential value. Re-utilising this by-product in food development and recovering its high value-added compounds could greatly contribute to food waste avoidance and achieving sustainable food development. Currently, the utilisation of PSOC as a novel alternative plant-based protein source has exhibited high potential. Nevertheless, to maximise the potential of PSCO in plant-based protein sector, more studies are needed on extraction methods, digestibility, allergenicity, and sensory properties. On the other hand, the nutritional profile of PSOC indicates its potential value as a novel food ingredient and has been successfully applied in the development of bakery products to enrich their nutritional value. Future studies could focus on the expansion of a wider range of PSOC products and the nutrient bioavailability of reformulated foods to satisfy the requirements of specific markets and provide more nutritional information to consumers.

passages.text: Clinical characteristics of female Fabry disease patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with mid-ventricular obstruction

Fabry disease (FD) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by mutations in GLA, which encodes alpha-galactosidase A (GLA). The loss or reduced activity of GLA leads to damage to multiple organs, resulting in the intracellular accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in various organs, including the heart, kidneys, and nervous system. Pathological changes in the heart typically result in concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an intractable disease characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction and is typically characterized by asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy. We performed a causative gene analysis in patients with a rare subtype of HCM, HCM with mid-ventricular obstruction (HCM-MVO), and identified four patients with different pathogenic variants of GLA, which were clinically confirmed as FD. All four patients with FD and rare HCM-MVO morphology were female, and all cases involved the classical form of the disease. Three cases in whom lymphocyte Lyso-Gb3 was measured showed a marked decrease in Lyso-Gb3 after initiating enzyme replacement therapy (ERT). However, even after ERT, myocardial involvement worsened in the long term, and two patients experienced fatal arrhythmias. Therefore, it is difficult to determine the efficacy of myocardial involvement in FD using a lymphocyte-based Lyso-Gb3 assay system. In addition, none of these female patients had renal dysfunction, indicating a different pattern of organ damage compared with that previously reported in male patients.
Highlights
Female patient with Fabry disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy complicated by Fabry disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with mid-ventricular obstruction.
Introduction

Fabry disease (FD) (OMIN #301500) is an X-linked inherited disorder of glucosylceramide metabolism. It is characterized by the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in various organs, including the heart, due to a deficiency or absence of alpha-galactosidase A activity caused by an abnormality in the GLA gene, the gene encoding alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-gal) on the X chromosome. Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), similar to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), is observed in cardiac lesions, and diastolic dysfunction is also present. FD in HCM is reported to occur in approximately 1 % of patients, although the severity of symptoms and timing of onset vary according to sex.

A subtype of HCM, apical aneurysm, and mid-ventricular obstruction (HCM-MVO) account for 9 %-10 % of HCM cases. HCM-MVO is defined as a subtype of HCM with mid-ventricular lumen narrowing and a pressure gradient of >=30 mmHg in continuous wave Doppler imaging. HCM-MVO is associated with a high rate of ventricular mass formation due to myocardial degeneration and thinning in the entire apical region (approximately 30 %). This may lead to the development of lethal ventricular arrhythmias originating in this region and systemic embolisms, including stroke caused by thrombus formation in the ventricular mass, and is a poor prognostic indicator. This group of patients has a poor prognosis. The etiology of apical aneurysm/HCM-MVO has not been elucidated, although it has been reported to be a high-risk group with a higher risk of death than regular HCM.

Because these two diseases are very rare, there have been very few reports of FD and HCM-MVO complications. In this report, we describe four cases of complications related to FD and HCM-MVO (FD-MVO). This study was approved by the ethics committees of local institutional review boards.
Patients report

All FD-MVO cases we encountered were female. In all cases, the patients were diagnosed with HCM in their 40s or later (average age, 51 years), followed by several years of follow-up (average age, 7 years) before the diagnosis of FD. All patients underwent enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) as soon as possible after being diagnosed with FD.
Case 1

At age 49, case 1 was diagnosed with HCM, and at age 58, GLA (NM_000169.3) c.329delC (p.Pro110Leufs*11) was identified, leading to a diagnosis of FD. At the time of FD diagnosis, her subjective symptoms were NYHA class II. At age 59, she started ERT with agalsidase alpha, but heart damage progressed. At age 65, she developed cerebral infarction, followed by ventricular tachycardia (VT) with shock, and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) was inserted. She has since been continuing ERT with agalsidase beta. Furthermore, the FD-associated acroparesthesia was markedly improved by ERT.
Case 2

Case 2 was diagnosed with HCM at age 68; at the time of diagnosis, she already exhibited HCM-MVO morphology with an apical aneurysm. Genetic testing was performed to identify GLA c.520 T > C (p.Cys174Arg), rs181562693, leading to a diagnosis of FD. Her subjective symptoms at the time of FD diagnosis were New York Heart Association Class II. An ICD was inserted because of frequent slow VT with heart failure at age 69, and the treatment was changed from ERT to pharmacological chaperone therapy at age 72. Mild cerebral infarction developed during FD therapy; however, the presentation was mild and did not interfere with daily activities.
Case 3

Case 3 was diagnosed with HCM at age 45. The disease worsened to HCM-MVO at age 59, and genetic testing for close examination identified GLA c.550 T > A (p.Tyr184Asn), which led to the diagnosis of FD. At the time of FD diagnosis, her symptoms were classified as NYHA class II. ERT with agalsidase alpha was initiated promptly after diagnosis, but she was switched to drug chaperone therapy at age 62 due to a variant of GLA that indicated the need for chaperone therapy. Chaperone therapy was successfully continued; however, at the age of 65 years, atrial fibrillation developed and heart failure developed. Her FD-associated symptoms, such as acroparesthesia, lessened with age, and her gastrointestinal symptoms improved with continued ERT.
Case 4

Case 4 was diagnosed with HCM and HCM-MVO at 38 and 44 years of age, respectively. A myocardial biopsy conducted for further examination of HCM-MVO revealed accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in cardiomyocytes, raising the suspicion of FD. Genetic testing identified a novel variant, GLA c.785G > C (p.Trp262Ser), which was associated with decreased alpha-gal activity, confirming the diagnosis of FD. At that point, the patient's heart failure symptoms worsened, and the NYHA classified him as Class III. After being diagnosed with FD, ERT with agalsidase beta was started immediately; however, the cardiac symptoms progressed, and the patient presented with HCM-MVO with apical aneurysm. In addition, atrial fibrillation occurred because of cardiac conduction defects, resulting in heart failure symptoms, and pulmonary vein isolation was performed using catheter ablation. Her FD symptoms, including acroparesthesia, become less severe with age.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging findings in four cases.

In all cases, the left ventricular wall is diffusely thickened and there is luminal stenosis with a pressure gradient in the mid-ventricle. Cases 1, 2, and 4 showed ventricular aneurysm formation with thinning of the apex.
Fig. 1

In all cases, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed MVO-HCM morphology and delayed contrast indicated findings suggestive of FD; thus, FD was suspected, and the definitive diagnosis was triggered by cardiac lesions (Fig. 1).
Delayed contrast images in all cases showed a strong delayed contrast effect in the mid-layer at the base of the posterior lateral wall, as indicated by white squares.

However, in all cases, the cardiac lesions progressed to a high-risk group for HCM-MVOs, accompanied by an apical aneurysm. Case 2-4) started ERT after developing HCM-MVO and showed a marked decrease in Lyso-Gb3 levels after ERT (Fig. 2).

Despite continued treatment with ERT, Case 1 developed HCM-MVO after ERT initiation. Cases 2, 3, and 4, in which a marked decrease in Lyso-Gb3 levels was observed with ERT, also developed cardiac symptoms after ERT initiation, and all three patients developed tachyarrhythmia-induced heart failure symptoms. In addition, two of the four patients developed fatal arrhythmias after ERT initiation and underwent ICD implantation (Table 1).
Discussion

The clinical course of FD varies according to disease type and patient sex. In male patients (hemizygotes) with classical FD, clinical symptoms appear across all organs of the body owing to defective or markedly low enzymatic activity of alpha-gal activity. In contrast, in female heterozygotes, clinical manifestations vary from asymptomatic to severe, depending on the rate of inactivation of the X chromosome carrying the mutant allele. Although the four female patients with FD in this study also showed progression of myocardial lesions to the HCM-MVO phenotype, eGFR was preserved in all four cases and renal dysfunction was almost nonexistent, a major difference from FD-MVO in males.

In addition, the enzyme activity of individual cells can be normal or decreased, while alpha-gal activity in plasma and organs varies, resulting in different phenotypes in different organs. However, none of the patients in this study showed improvement in myocardial lesions with ERT, and two patients developed fatal arrhythmias while continuing ERT. Therefore, determining the efficacy of myocardial therapy for FD using a lymphocyte-based measurement system is difficult.

The present case series included female heterozygous FD patients with the HCM-MVO phenotype. These patients were diagnosed with FD after HCM diagnosis, while ERT was initiated after cardiac lesion progression. Despite Lyso-Gb3 values demonstrating good compliance with ERT, myocardial damage progressed, and half of them underwent ICD implantation for secondary prevention.

Cardiomyopathy due to FD is arrhythmogenic, with a high rate of ICD use. It is also difficult to determine the efficacy of therapies, including ERT, for cardiac lesions, and there are reports of a greater slope of the left ventricular mass index (LVMI) in female patients with FD who develop LVH. In addition, the incidence of LVMI was higher in women than in men with FD.

In general, organ damage occurs approximately 10 years later in women than in men, and there are fewer cases of progression in each organ in women than in men. Therefore, European and US guidelines recommend early initiation of ERT in male patients with FD; however, in female patients, ERT is typically not indicated, unless serious clinical complications are evident. In Japan, the indications for ERT have not been systematically validated and are determined individually at each institution. However, there have been reports that the severity of myocardial damage does not correlate with the degree of cardiac hypertrophy in female FD patients. In some cases, such as this case, the patient progressed to FD-MVO and developed a fatal arrhythmia after ERT initiation. In addition, the results of exome sequencing, performed in all four cases, detected no genetic variants associated with cardiomyopathy that could cause complications or poor prognosis, except for the identified GLA variant. As such, predicting treatment response or cardiac lesion severity using variant information or lymphocyte-based measurement systems such as the Lyso-Gb3 assay remains difficult. Therefore, although the optimal timing of ERT initiation in female FD patients is controversial, both from the perspective of cost-effectiveness and clinical challenges, such as individual variability in symptoms and the burden of lifelong treatment, it is necessary to consider the timing of treatment initiation to prevent the progression of myocardial damage before cardiac lesions become prominent and to follow-up for monitoring sudden death even after treatment initiation.
Conclusion

The clinical course of FD depends on disease type and sex. In general, males tend to experience more organ damage than females, and there are fewer cases of progression in each organ in females than in males. However, some female patients diagnosed with FD after the onset of cardiac symptoms may develop fatal arrhythmias after ERT initiation, resulting in poor prognosis of MVO morphology. The timing of treatment initiation and follow-up regimen for female patients with FD should be considered.

passages.text: Prostaglandins: Biological Action, Therapeutic Aspects, and Pathophysiology of Autism Spectrum Disorders

Esterified ARA on the inner surface of the cell membrane is hydrolyzed to its free form by phospholipase A2 (PLA2), which is further metabolized by COXs and lipoxygenases (LOXs) and cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes. PGs produce detrimental effects due to their proinflammatory properties. The generation of prostaglandin (PG)G2 and PGH2 is triggered by cyclooxygenase (COX) isozymes such as COX-1 and COX-2. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is significantly elevated in ASD. Considerable data indicate that COX enzymes and their metabolites of ARA play important roles in the initiation and development of human neurodevelopmental diseases. The involvement of disrupted COX2/PGE2 signaling in ASD pathology in changing neuronal cell behavior and the expression of ASD-related genes and proteins is due to disrupted COX2/PGE2 signaling. Prostacyclin (PGI2) is synthesized from arachidonic acid by metabolic-pathway-dependent cyclooxygenase (COX) and synthesized in a primary step of ARA transformation (PGG2, PGH2), by degradation of the abovementioned prostaglandins.
1. Introduction

Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) plays a fundamental role in the production of prostaglandins (PGs) by releasing arachidonic acid (ARA). Esterified ARA on the inner surface of the cell membrane is hydrolyzed to its free form by PLA2. PGs are synthesized from ARA by the action of cyclooxygenases (COXs) and terminal PG synthases. Cellular and mitochondrial membrane phospholipids provide the synthesis and release of PGs in response to chemical and noxious stimuli. Abnormalities in the COX-2/prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) pathway due to genetic or environmental factors have been linked to autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).

Deficient dietary supplementation and exposure to oxidative stress, infections, and inflammation may disrupt signaling of the PGE2 pathway and contribute to ASD. The structure and establishment of two critical protective barriers in the brain during early development are influenced by environmental factors, such as exposure to chemicals in air pollution, pesticides, and consumer products. These factors may disrupt PGE2 signaling, thereby increasing the risk of developing ASD. Additionally, it is crucial to understand how these exogenous agents are capable of crossing protective barriers, highlighting the importance of avoiding or limiting exposure to these factors during vulnerable periods of development.
2. Metabolites of Prostaglandins (PGs)

Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is an endogenous lipid mediator of inflammation. Its production is regulated by the rate-limiting upstream enzyme cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), regulating membrane excitability in various forms of synaptic plasticity. Spontaneous glutamatergic synaptic activity regulates constitutive neuronal COX-2 expression.

Esterified ARA on the inner surface of the cell membrane is metabolized to a free form by PLA2 and further metabolized by COXs, lipoxygenases (LOXs), and cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes into a spectrum of bioactive mediators (Figure 1). The COX enzymes and ARA metabolites play important roles in the initiation and development of human diseases. The generation of PGG2 and PGH2 is initiated by COX isozymes, including COX-1 and COX-2, which are derived from ARA through the enzymatic activities of COX and peroxidase.. ARA is metabolized to eicosanoids, including PGs, leukotrienes, and thromboxanes, which are proinflammatory molecules, triggered by oxidative stress. These lipid mediators play critical roles in the initiation, maintenance, and modulation of neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. Therefore, the ARA metabolic pathways are effective targets for managing inflammatory-related diseases. Eicosanoids play a role in neural functioning, including sleep induction (PGD2), long-term potentiation, spatial learning, and synaptic plasticity (PGE2).
3. Role of Prostaglandins
PGF2a and thromboxane A2 (TXA2) are endogenous ARA metabolites, influencing diverse physiological processes such as inflammation via activation of PGF2a receptor (FP) and TXA2 receptor (TP).

Endogenous and exogenous PGs have beneficial effects on cellular protection, sleep regulation, and blood flow enhancement. PGs and their receptors are intimately involved in many homeostatic activities and are beneficial in the proper functioning of the central nervous system (CNS), as they are the structural basis for ligand recognition and the activation of prostanoid receptors. The various roles of PGs indicate destructive or neuroprotective features of these ubiquitous endogenous mediators.

PGE2 and PGD2, which are biosynthesized from ARA by enzymatic cleavage of membrane phospholipids in response to various stimuli, play key roles in multiple brain pathophysiological processes, including modulation of synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation, and sleep promotion. Prostacyclin 12 (PGI2) is synthesized from ARA by metabolic-pathway-dependent COX. PGD2 is synthesized in the primary step of ARA transformation (PGG2, PGH2) by degradation of the abovementioned PGs but is not presented physiologically, and may be chemically generated (PGK2, PGL2). PGG2 and PGH2 are produced from ARA, which act as inflammatory cells.

Regarding the association among PUFAs and long-chain metabolites, including gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), dihomo-GLA (DGLA), ARA, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and DHA, other PG products (PGE1 and PGI2) and lipoxins (LXs) may have anti-inflammatory actions.
4. PEG2 and Glutamate Activity

PGE2 inhibits the neuronal activity of the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray via attenuation of glutamatergic synaptic inputs. Glutamate excitotoxicity was proposed to participate in the propagation of ASD. Palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) is an endocannabinoid proven to prevent glutamatergic toxicity and inhibit inflammatory responses simultaneously. PGE2 is a physiological signal for inducing glutamate release from subventricular zone in astrocytes, thus being important for moderating neuroblast survival and proliferation.

Therefore, PEG 2E may be closely related to glutamate toxication, contributing to the development of ASD.

Glutamate excitotoxicity was proposed to participate in the propagation of ASD. Abnormalities in glutamate and GABA signaling have been hypothesized to underlie ASD symptoms and may form a therapeutic target in humans with ASD and animal models of the disorder. In humans with ASD, glutamate concentration was reduced in the striatum in correlation with the severity of social symptoms. GABA levels were not altered in either brain region. Glutamate/GABA abnormalities in the corticostriatal circuitry may be a key pathological mechanism in ASD and may be linked to alterations in the neuroligin-neurexin signaling complex. Adults with idiopathic ASD have lower glutamate concentrations in the striatum compared to controls, suggesting a correlation with the severity of social impairment.. The findings on humans and rodent models of ASD are suggestive of a region-specific imbalance slanted toward reduced excitation.

In summary, blood glutamate levels might be a potential biomarker of ASD. Additionally, imbalance between excitatory (glutamatergic) and inhibitory (GABAergic) mechanisms underlies the behavioral characteristics of ASD.
5. Association of Prostaglandins with Other Amino Acids

GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission is critical for the regulation of brain rhythm and spontaneous neuronal activities during neurodevelopment via an abnormal excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) neurotransmission ratio implicated in the pathogenesis of ASD. Current candidate genes induce dysfunction of GABAergic transmission by affecting the transcription of GABA-A receptor (GABA-AR) and causing presynaptic GABA release, the formation of GABAergic synapses, and synaptic structure-mediated transmission.

Impaired GABAergic signaling during brain development is a crucial event implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental diseases. In addition, 15q duplication mice (a model for ASD with human chromosome 15q11-q13 paternal duplication) exhibited facilitated activity-induced long-term potentiation (LTP) of glutamate synapses onto layer-5 pyramidal neurons and a reduced number of inhibitory synapses, indicating that shifted E/I balance is implicated in autism.

GABAergic dysfunction could be a downstream consequence of mutations in genes and not directly be involved in GABA transmission because the proper development and function of GABA synapses rely on numerous signaling and scaffolding proteins. Currently known candidate genes of ASD include transcription factors, scaffolding proteins, receptors, and signaling pathways. GABA functions as an excitatory neurotransmitter during embryonic development and may play a role in the pathophysiology of fragile X syndrome. ASD models have an abnormal excitatory GABA inhibitory shift during delivery with elevated intracellular chloride levels and maintenance of higher levels of excitatory GABA, promoting glutamic acid activity and gamma oscillatory activity.

The transition of inhibitory to excitatory neurotransmission during early brain development might be s pathological mechanism of the imbalance in the E/I ratio and GABA disturbance involved in ASD. Specific brain regions and developmental time windows play a critical role in understanding the mechanisms of GABA involved in ASD.

Valproic acid (VPA), as a broad-spectrum antiepileptic drug, has a significant facilitative effect on the GABAergic neurotransmission system. Impaired GABAergic inhibitory transmission has been observed in prenatal VPA exposure-induced autism models. Prenatal maternal immune activation might have effect on long-lasting GABAergic changes relevant to ASD.

In summary, duplications of the E3 ubiquitin ligase gene UBE3A and three non-imprinted GABA-AR genes located at 15q11.2-q13.1 are associated with autistic phenotype behavioral deficits. This is linked to the structural chromosomal protein MeCP2, a homeobox transcription factor involved in the synthesis and modification of synaptic proteins crucial for GABAergic synaptic function. Neuroligins might affect the formation of neural connectivity via affecting the early postnatal transition of excitatory GABA. Pharmacological intervention with agonists targeting specific GABA receptors alleviates ASD-related behavioral abnormalities in animal models.

GABAergic synaptic transmission dysfunction in specific neurons or circuitry during the developmental stage might underlie the pathophysiology of ASD. Impaired GABAergic transmission might be a critical etiology of imbalance of the E/I ratio involved in the development of ASD. GABA can shift from "excitatory" to "inhibitory" and play a critical role in the subtle regulation of neuronal networks during critical developmental stages, and altered excitation might be secondary to reduced inhibition and GABA dysfunction.

PGE2 potently depresses GABAergic-inhibitory synaptic transmission on parvocellular neuroendocrine cells (PNCs). Using pharmacological approaches via the actions of presynaptic EP3 receptors potently depresses GABA release onto parvocellular neuroendocrine cells (PNCs).

PGE2 acts at a presynaptic locus to decrease the probability of GABA release. The PEG receptor EP3 subtype of the PGE2 receptor mediates the actions of PGE2 on GABA synapses. PGE2, via actions of presynaptic EP3 receptors, potently depresses GABA release onto PNCs, providing a plausible mechanism for the disinhibition of HPA axis output during inflammation. The effects of PGE2 on GABA synapses provide strong evidence indicating that PGE2 potently inhibits GABAergic synaptic transmission (eIPSCs, sIPSCs and mIPSCs. The PGE2-induced GABA synapse depression is primarily attributable to a decrease in the release of vesicles from presynaptic terminals. PGE2-attenuated GABA release is independent of the potential firing of presynaptic neurons and its receptors expressed on the axonal terminals in the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus.
6. Prostaglandin Signaling in Pathophysiology of ASD
6.1. PEG2-COX2 I ASD

The presence of an abnormal COX-PGE2 signaling pathway due to genetic or environmental causes may be linked to ASD. The brain at embryonic day 16 (E16) is particularly susceptible to the influence of biological pathways involving various ASD-associated genes. Crosstalk between the COX2-PGE2 and Wnt pathways during early brain development may play a crucial role in the pathophysiology of ASD models.

Higher levels of PGE2 increased the Wnt-dependent motility and proliferation of neuroectodermal stem cells and modified the expression of Wnt genes linked to ASD. PGE2 signaling also converges with the Wnt canonical pathway in the developing mouse brain after maternal exposure to PGE2 at the onset of neurogenesis. Since prenatal exposure to PGE2 affects the Wnt pathway at the level of beta-catenin, the major downstream regulator of Wnt may be related to gene transcription. PGE2 can influence the expression level of genes from the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, including Mmp7, Wnt2, and Wnt3a, linked to ASD. The convergence of PGE2 with the Wnt canonical pathway was apparent due to higher levels of PKA-activated phosphorylated beta-catenin (Ser552) and active non-phospho beta-catenin (Ser33/37/Thr41) (Figure 2).
6.2. Mechanisms of PEG2

Importantly, changes in the matrilysin activity level, also known as matrix metalloproteinase-7 (Mmp7), due to exposure to PGE2 may have potential consequences at various stages of the developing brain. Abnormal PGE2 levels in the mouse brain during the developmental period may interfere with the Wnt pathway via phosphorylation of beta-catenin at multiple sites, which can lead to differential expression of crucial neurodevelopmental genes. Exposure to maternal PGE2 at a critical time can have an effect on the expression of Wnt target genes during prenatal (E16 and E19) brain development.
7. PGs in the Pathophysiology of ASD

PGE2 is an endogenous lipid molecule that plays an important role in normal brain development. COX2 is the primary regulator of PGE2 production. In a study by El-Ansary, A, the significant decrease in their ratio (COX2/PGE2) as a marker of lipid metabolism signaling in autistic individuals compared to controls may be due to altered COX-2 enzyme kinetics in ASD patients. PGE2 regulates the effects of Wnt signaling through cAMP/PKA activity, and it may directly regulate beta-catenin destruction by the nucleosome and subsequent proteins available for transcriptional activation. ASD patients with an abnormal COX-2/PGE2 signaling pathway have a significantly lower ratio, despite higher levels of independent variables. The combined ROC of COX/PGE2 and anti-nucleosome autoantibodies, along with their proven roles in impaired lipid metabolism, autoimmunity, and glutamate excitotoxicity as the disorder's three etiological mechanisms, raises the possibility that these variables could be used for an early diagnosis of ASD and certain co-morbidities seen in ASD patients.

PGE2 interacts with canonical Wnt signaling through PKA and PI-3K in neuroectodermal (NE-4C) stem cells. There is a possible association between prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), and microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 (mPGES-1).

PGE2 treatment causes changes in cell behavior, such as an increase in components of cell motility and proliferation, as well as the expression of Wnt target genes in Wnt-activated cell line NE-4C stem cells in human colorectal adenoma and carcinoma cells. PGE2 increases the final distance and path length traveled in the migration of Wnt-activated neuroectodermal stem NE-4C cells and alters the phenotype of Wnt-treated cells. Wnt/beta-catenin signaling occurs through a complex, highly regulated pathway that involves the phosphorylation of multiple sites on beta-catenin, which may promote its degradation or activation and subsequent nuclear internalization. PGE2 treatment administered to Wnt-activated cells increased the expression of non-phosphorylated (active) beta-catenin (Ser33/37/Thr41) protein. PGE2 signaling may modulate GSK3beta activity, although this remains to be determined. Our gene expression results show a potential interaction of PGE2 and the canonical Wnt pathway in the nervous system and provide further evidence for a link to ASD. We show that PGE2 interacts with canonical Wnt signaling through the phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI-3K) pathway or the protein kinase A (PKA) pathway. PKA and PI-3K produce reported behavioral changes in cell motility and proliferation, as well as gene expression. Specifically, we found that inhibiting these PGE2 downstream pathway kinases, PKA and PI-3K, with H89 and Wort, respectively, reduced the effect of PGE2. Increased PGE2 signaling can modify cell migration, proliferation behavior, and gene expression in Wnt-activated NE-4C stem cells. PGE2 can affect Wnt-dependent cell behaviors and gene expression in neuroectodermal stem cells through PKA and PI-3K. Aberrant PGE2 and Wnt signaling have been linked to ASD. These aberrations may be potential mechanisms in the genesis of neurodevelopment disorders like ASD.

passages.text: A proteomic analysis revealed eight signaling pathways that were significantly dysregulated in ASD patients; three of these (transendothelial leukocyte migration, antigen processing and presentation, and graft vs. host disease) were associated with the neuroimmune response. The metabolism of tryptophan related to the neuroimmune response play a potential role in ASD. Integrated proteome and metabolome analysis showed that six signaling pathways were significantly enriched in ASD patients, three of which were correlated with impaired neuroinflammation (glutathione metabolism, metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450, and transendothelial migration of leukocytes). PGE2 levels have been associated with the inflammatory response in ASD. Therefore, the neuroimmune response in ASD provides potential biomarkers as targets for early intervention.

Many studies have reported that neuroinflammation, which is also observed in neurodegenerative disorders, is implicated in the pathophysiology of ASD. Moreover, the effect of altered microbiota on neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation in the pathological factors of ASD has been studied. The PGE2 level was considerably greater in patients with ASD than in controls. An association between the impairment of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (LCPUFA) metabolism and both proinflammation and oxidative stress in the etiopathology of ASD has been reported. Therefore, omega-3 LCPUFA supplementation ameliorates proinflammation and oxidative stress-related symptoms.

ASD patients exhibit significantly higher levels of the measured parameters compared to neurotypical controls, with the exception of EP2 receptors, which showed an opposite trend. Although the measured parameters did not correlate with the severity of social and cognitive dysfunction, PGE2, COX-2, and microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 (mPGES-1) were associated with sensory processing dysfunction.

The positive correlation between PGE2, COX-2, and mPGES-1 confirms the role of the PGE2 pathway and neuroinflammation in the etiology of ASD, and the possibility of using PGE2, COX-2, and mPGES-1 as biomarkers of autism severity has been reported. PGE2 is an endogenous lipid molecule involved in normal brain development. PGs include PGD2, and PGE2 interacts with G protein-coupled receptors, presenting new opportunities for transformative therapeutics in neuropsychiatric disorders. COX-2- mice express increased hyperactivity, repetitive behavior, and social abnormality. The COX2/PGE2 pathway changes neuronal cell behavior and the expression of ASD-related genes and proteins. Mouse models of ASD are related to disrupted COX2/PGE2 signaling. PGE2 activates the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, and the upregulated genes have been previously reported to be associated with ASD. PGE2 signaling also converges with the Wnt canonical pathway in the developing mouse brain after maternal exposure to PGE2 at the level of beta-catenin or through PKA and PI-3K in neuroectodermal (NE-4C) stem cells. Additionally, prenatal exposure to PGE2 affects the Wnt pathway at the level of beta-catenin, which is the major downstream regulator of Wnt-dependent gene transcription. Regarding the function of PGE2 and Wnt in the pathophysiology of ASD, PGE2 can affect Wnt-dependent cell activities and gene expression in neuroectodermal stem cells through the interplay of camp/protein kinase A (PKA) and phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) signaling. PGE2 treatment elicits changes in cell activities through increased components of cell motility and proliferation, as well as the expression of Wnt target genes in Wnt-activated NE-4C stem cells (Iwasa). PGE2 increases the final distance and path length traveled, as well as the average speed of migration, in Wnt-activated neuroectodermal stem NE-4C cells. These changes in cell motility and proliferation activity could have critical effects on the early development of the nervous system. The system of cellular events, including migration and proliferation, occurs during developmental windows. Changed migration and proliferation due to irregular gene expression during embryonic development may be potential mechanisms in the genesis of neurodevelopment disorders, such as ASD. These crucial neurobiological processes are required for the formation of complex layered structures in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum.

8. PG-Related Signaling Pathways

Wnt signaling modulates neurite outgrowth, axon growth and guidance, dendritic development and arborization, synapse formation, and synaptic plasticity. Moreover, Wnt signaling is crucial in the specification and differentiation of neuronal precursors in the midbrain and forebrain. Wnt signaling is included in a myriad of regulatory processes in the development and organization of the nervous system.

Wnt proteins are a key factor in neural tube formation, neuronal migration, and differentiation. Defective Wnt signaling could contribute to the pathogenesis of psychiatric disorders, including ASD. Particularly, Wnt2, located in the putative speech and language region at chromosome 7q31-33, has been identified as a susceptibility gene for ASD. The interaction of the Wnt and PGE2 pathways occurs in NE-4C stem cells: alterations in the levels of PGE2 via endogenous and exogenous means greatly affect nervous system development. Wnt/beta-catenin signaling occurs through a complex, highly regulated pathway that involves the phosphorylation of multiple sites on beta-catenin, which may promote its degradation or activation and subsequent nuclear internalization. COX-2 is a crucial mediator of inflammation and prostanoid signaling. The efficacy of the COX-2 inhibitor drug, celecoxib, as an adjunctive therapy in the treatment of ASD has been indicated. Mmp-9, a membrane of the matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) family, is also important in neuronal development. Elevated levels of MMP9 protein were found in the amniotic fluid of individuals with ASD.

PGE2 is the signaling molecule converted by COX-2. The effect of COX-2-KI on microglial density and morphology may be important in the developing brain. COX-2-deficient (COX-2-KI) mice exhibit sex-dependent molecular changes in the brain and ASD-related behaviors. Microglia may be influenced by the surroundings, affecting the development of the healthy brain with synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, and phagocytosis. COX-2-KI female rats were affected on gestational day 19 (G19), showing increased microglial density, altered percentages of amoeboid and ramified microglia, changes in branch length (reduced or increased), and decreased branching networks in a region-specific manner. G19 COX-2-KI male rats showed increased microglial density, a higher percentage of ramified microglia, and increased branch counts. Therefore, COX-2 deficiency in the ASD mouse model affects microglia morphology in a sex-, region-, and stage-dependent manner.

As an endogenous lipid molecule, PGE2 is essential for normal brain development. Autism-related behaviors were prominent in male COX-2- mice in most behavioral tests. The involvement of disrupted COX2/PGE2 signaling in ASD pathology has been reported with age-related differences and a greater impact on men. COX-2- mice exhibited increased hyperactivity, repetitive behavior, and social abnormality. The COX2/PGE2 pathway changed neuronal cell behavior and the expression of ASD-related genes and proteins. Mouse models have shown disrupted COX2/PGE2 signaling. Aberrant cell migration and proliferation are pathophysiologic mechanisms affecting the brain and may contribute to the occurrence of neurodevelopment disorders.
